questions.question: A workload needs to read ConfigMaps in one namespace. Which permission approach follows least privilege?

options.text: Grant cluster-admin access to every workload.
Grant its ServiceAccount only the required ConfigMap read permissions in that namespace.
Disable authorization for the cluster.
Give the workload a human administrator's credentials.

questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the resource access and operations the workload needs. A namespaced Role and RoleBinding can provide this access to its ServiceAccount.

questions.question: What is the role of a Kubernetes ServiceAccount?

options.text: To provide an identity for processes running in Pods.
To provide permanent storage for application data.
To expose every Pod to the public internet.
To automatically grant administrator permissions.

questions.explanation: A ServiceAccount provides a workload identity. Authentication identifies the account, while authorization determines what that identity is allowed to do.

questions.question: What is required for Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules to be enforced?

options.text: Every Pod must run as root.
All Services must use public IP addresses.
All namespaces must have the same name.
The cluster must use a network implementation that supports NetworkPolicy enforcement.

questions.explanation: Creating a NetworkPolicy resource alone is insufficient if the cluster's network implementation does not support enforcing it.

questions.question: Which configuration helps reduce a container's privileges when the application supports it?

options.text: Enable privileged mode for every container.
Mount the host's entire filesystem with write access.
Run as a non-root user, disallow privilege escalation and drop unnecessary Linux capabilities.
Share administrator credentials between all containers.

questions.explanation: These settings restrict container privileges and reduce potential impact if an application is compromised. They should be tested against the application's requirements.

questions.question: An application starts returning more errors after a deployment. Which investigation is most useful?

options.text: Correlate error metrics, application logs and deployment timing.
Delete all logs to reduce noise.
Assume CPU usage alone explains every error.
Disable monitoring until the errors stop.

questions.explanation: Metrics reveal changes and trends, while logs provide details about failures. Comparing them with deployment events helps identify likely causes.

questions.question: An application is temporarily unable to serve requests, but restarting it would not help. Which probe is intended to signal that it should stop receiving normal Service traffic?

options.text: A liveness probe configured to restart it immediately.
A readiness probe.
A container image signature.
A resource limit.

questions.explanation: A failed readiness probe marks the container as not ready, affecting Pod readiness and normal Service routing. Readiness failure does not itself restart the container.

questions.question: What does a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler typically adjust?

options.text: The application's source code.
The number of namespaces.
The container image's filesystem.
The number of replicas in a scalable workload, based on observed metrics.

questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling changes the number of workload replicas. It differs from vertical scaling, which changes the resources allocated to individual instances.

questions.question: An autoscaler requests more application replicas, but the new Pods remain Pending because no node has sufficient available capacity for their resource requests. What should you investigate?

options.text: Whether changing the Pod names will create more CPU.
Whether disabling logs guarantees scheduling.
Node capacity, Pod resource requests and whether node scaling can provide suitable capacity.
Whether adding more replicas alone will increase node memory.

questions.explanation: Increasing replica count does not create node resources. Scheduling requires suitable capacity, so resource requests and node scaling must be considered together.
